newsitem.title: USA: U.S. NRC chief discusses deregulation changes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. NRC chief discusses deregulation changes.

text.p: The restructuring of the electric utility industry will force regulators to scrutinize utilities' financial status to see how it affects the safety of their nuclear power plants, the head of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission said Wednesday.
"We're interested in how economic pressures may affect safety and maintenance," NRC chairwoman Shirley Jackson told an energy policy group.
"We will need to look at their financial status and financial reliability relative to our issues," she said.
But nuclear power plants can be operated safely in a less regulated electric power industry, Jackson said.
"Protection of public health and safety is entirely compatible with a deregulated environment," she said.
Jackson said the commission is looking into measures to improve its ability to collect financial information.

The commission also is looking at ways to ensure that utilities have funds available to cover costs of decommissioning nuclear plants ahead of schedule if the plants are uncompetitive in the deregulated environment, she said.
Utilities collect funds through rates to cover future decommissioning costs, but there are concerns on how those costs would be covered if plants were closed down prematurely.
Jackson also said the NRC was having "preliminary discussions" on its role in the Energy Department's plan to combine surplus plutonium with conventional nuclear fuel to use in nuclear plants.
That option is one of two under consideration by the Clinton administration to try to dispose of plutonium left over from the nuclear weapons program.

Jackson said it was premature for the NRC to consider adding staff and resources for potential additional duties of monitoring transportation and security of the plutonium and the mixed fuel called MOX.
"It's an evolving situation, but it's one that we're highly sensitive to," she said.
The Energy Department said it was pursuing a "dual-track" approach to disposing of the plutonioum, and also would solidify it in glass for long-term storage.
The department said it was pursuing both options to give itself flexibility in case one plan proved less workable.
